name: Nehemiah
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: This is the story of Nehemiah, Hacaliah’s son, in his own words. It was the month of Kislev (in November–December) in the king’s twentieth year. At that time I was living in Susa, the royal fortress.{a}
One of my brothers, Hanani, arrived from Judah with some other men. I asked them for news of the Jews there, the ones who had escaped being taken captive. I also asked about Jerusalem.
They told me, “Those who survived and are left in the province are in deep trouble. People look down on them. Jerusalem’s wall has holes broken in it, and its gates have been burned down.”
Hearing this, I sat down and cried. For days I grieved. I went without food and kept praying to the God of heaven.
“Yahweh, God of heaven,” I prayed, “you are great, and you fill us with awe. You keep your promises. Those who love you and do what you command receive your faithful love.

Please open your eyes and your ears. Day and night I, your servant, keep praying for Israel’s people, who serve you. Hear me now. I admit that we Israelites have sinned against you. My family and I are part of that sin.
We have done terrible wrong to you. We failed to keep the commands, rules, and laws you gave to Moses, your servant.
Please call to mind the warning you gave through Moses, who served you. You said, ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations.

But if you turn around and obey what I command, I will gather you home. You may be scattered to the far edge of the sky, yet I will gather you from there. I will bring you to the place I chose as the home for my Name.’{b}
They belong to you; they are your servants and your people. By your great power and your strong hand you set them free.

Lord, please hear my prayer. I am your servant. Hear, too, all your other servants, who are glad to honor your name. Let me succeed today. Make the king kind to me.” In those days I served the king as his cupbearer.{c}

notes.text: Nehemiah means “Yahweh comforts.” Hacaliah may mean “wait for Yahweh.” Kislev was the ninth month. The twentieth year of King Artaxerxes (2:1) was 446 BC. Susa was the winter capital of the Persian kings, in what is now southwest Iran.
See Leviticus 26:33; Deuteronomy 4:27; 12:5; 30:1-4.
The cupbearer tasted and served the king’s wine. He was a trusted official who was often close to the king.

verses.text: Four months later, in the month of Nisan (in March–April) of Artaxerxes’s twentieth year, it was my turn to serve the king his wine. I picked it up and gave it to him. Until that day I had never looked sad when I was with him.{a}
So the king asked, “Why so gloomy? You are not ill. This must be sadness deep in your heart.” That made me very afraid.
Still, I answered him, “Long live the king! How can I help looking sad? My ancestors are buried in that city, and now it lies wrecked. Fire has destroyed its gates.”
“Then what do you want?” the king asked me. Quickly I prayed to the God of heaven. Then I answered.
“If you are pleased with me, your servant, and if it seems good to you, here is my request. Send me off to Judah, to the city with my ancestors’ graves, so I can build it again.”
With the queen seated by his side, the king asked, “How long is the journey? When do you plan to return?” I told him how long I needed, and he was glad to let me go.{b}
Then I said, “If it pleases you, your majesty, give me letters to show the governors beyond the Euphrates River. Then they will let me travel through their lands until I get to Judah.{c}

Please give me a letter for Asaph too. He takes care of the royal forest. Ask him to give me logs for beams. I need them for the gates of the fortress next to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house where I will live.” Because my God’s kind hand was on me, the king gave me all I asked.{d}
So I traveled to the governors beyond the Euphrates and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent army commanders and soldiers on horses to travel with me.
Two men heard that I had come: Sanballat from Horon, and Tobiah, an official from Ammon. It greatly displeased them that a man had come to do good for the Israelites.{e}
I went on to Jerusalem. For three days I stayed there.
Then one night I got up and went out with a few men. I kept secret what my God had put into my heart for Jerusalem. We took no animals except the one I was riding.

In the dark I left by the Valley Gate and went toward the Dragon Spring and the Garbage Gate. I looked closely at Jerusalem’s walls, which had been torn down, and at its gates, which had been burned.{f}
From there I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool. But the path was too narrow for my animal to pass.
So I rode up the valley in the dark, still looking at the wall. Then I turned around and came back in through the Valley Gate.{g}

The city officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. Up to then I had said nothing to the Jews. I had not told the priests, the rich and powerful families, the officials, or anyone else who would do the work.

Then I spoke to them. “You see the bad shape we are in,” I said. “Jerusalem lies in ruins. Its gates have been burned. Come on, let’s build Jerusalem’s wall again, so people will stop making fun of us.”
I told them how my God had been kind to me and helped me. I also told them what the king had said. “Let’s start now!” they said. “Let’s build!” So they got ready to do this good work.

When Sanballat from Horon, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab got word of it, they mocked us and treated us with scorn. “What is this you are up to?” they asked. “Are you turning against the king?”{h}

I gave them this reply: “Success will come to us from the God of heaven. We serve him, and we will rise up and build. But you have nothing here in Jerusalem. You have no rights here, and no one will remember you here.”

notes.text: Nisan was the first month. This was the spring of 445 BC. Artaxerxes I was king of Persia 465-424 BC.
The Hebrew word may mean the king’s chief wife.
This was the Persian province west of the Euphrates. It included Syria and Judah.
The Hebrew word for “forest” is pardes, a Persian word for a royal park. The word “paradise” comes from it.
Sanballat means “the god Sin has given life.” He was governor of Samaria. “From Horon” probably means from Beth-horon. Tobiah means “Yahweh is good.” He was probably governor of Ammon.
Or “Jackal Spring.” The Hebrew calls it the “Dung Gate.”
This was the Kidron Valley, east of the city.
Geshem is known from an old silver bowl as a king of Kedar, a strong group of Arab tribes.

verses.text: The work began with Eliashib the high priest. The Sheep Gate was the job he and his fellow priests took on. They set it apart for God and hung its doors. The wall they dedicated reached past the Hundred Tower as far as Hananel’s Tower.{a}
Jericho’s men did the stretch beside them. Beyond that, Zaccur, Imri’s son, did the building.
Hassenaah’s family built the Fish Gate. They put its beams in place and hung its doors, with their bolts and bars.

Next along the wall, Meremoth repaired a section. He was Uriah’s son and Hakkoz’s grandson. Then Meshullam took the next part. He was Berechiah’s son and Meshezabel’s grandson. After him Zadok, Baana’s son, made repairs.
The people of Tekoa fixed the next part. But their important men refused to do the work their supervisors gave them.{b}
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah fixed the Old Gate. They set its beams in place and put up its doors, with bolts and bars.{c}
Beside them, men of Gibeon and Mizpah worked. They were led by Melatiah from Gibeon and Jadon from Meronoth. Their part reached to the place where the governor from beyond the Euphrates stayed.{d}
Uzziel, Harhaiah’s son, a goldsmith, worked on the next part. Hananiah, one of the perfume makers, worked after him. They restored Jerusalem’s wall as far as the Wide Wall.{e}
Rephaiah, Hur’s son, came next. He ruled half of the Jerusalem district.
Beyond him, Jedaiah, Harumaph’s son, worked on the wall facing his own house. Hattush, Hashabneiah’s son, worked beside Jedaiah.
Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab repaired another section, including the Tower of the Ovens.
Shallum, Hallohesh’s son, worked next to them, and his daughters helped him. The second half of the Jerusalem district was under his rule.

The Valley Gate was the work of Hanun and Zanoah’s people. They built it up again, and they hung the doors, fitting each with bars and bolts. After that they fixed 1,500 feet of the wall, reaching the Garbage Gate.{f}
The Garbage Gate itself was rebuilt by Malchijah, Rechab’s son, the ruler of the Beth-haccherem district. He put up its doors, with their bolts and bars.

Shallun, Col-hozeh’s son, ruler of the Mizpah district, fixed the Fountain Gate. He built it, put a roof over it, and hung its doors, with bolts and bars. Next he repaired the wall by the Pool of Shelah beside the royal garden, up to the stairs that lead down out of David’s City.{g}

Past him, Nehemiah son of Azbuk worked. He ruled half the Beth-zur district. He worked up to a spot facing the tombs of David, reaching the pool that people had dug and the building called the Warriors’ House.
Then came Levites. Rehum, Bani’s son, worked on the next part. Beside him Hashabiah, ruler of half the Keilah district, made repairs for his own district.
Their fellow Levites worked after them. They were led by Bavvai, Henadad’s son, ruler of the other half of the Keilah district.{h}
Next, Ezer, Jeshua’s son, the ruler of Mizpah, rebuilt another section. It faced the slope that goes up to the weapons storeroom, where the wall turns.
Baruch, Zabbai’s son, worked hard on the next stretch. It ran from the bend in the wall to the door of Eliashib the high priest’s house.{i}
Then Meremoth, son of Uriah and grandson of Hakkoz, fixed another section. It started at the entrance of Eliashib’s house and went to where the house ended.
Priests from the area around Jerusalem did the next repairs.{j}
In front of their own home, Benjamin and Hasshub did repairs. Then Azariah, son of Maaseiah and grandson of Ananiah, worked on the part next to his house.
Another section was rebuilt by Binnui, Henadad’s son. It went from Azariah’s house to the bend and the corner.
Palal, Uzai’s son, worked across from the bend and the tower that sticks out from the king’s upper palace near the guards’ courtyard. Then came Pedaiah, Parosh’s son,
and the temple servants whose homes were on Ophel. They worked up to a point facing the Water Gate on the east side and the tower that sticks out.{k}
The men of Tekoa took on a second section. It went from opposite the large tower that sticks out to the wall of Ophel.
Above the Horse Gate, the priests did the work. Each one fixed the part in front of his own house.
Zadok, Immer’s son, worked across from his house too. Next came Shemaiah, Shecaniah’s son, who guarded the East Gate.
After that, two men rebuilt another section: Hananiah, Shelemiah’s son, and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph. Then Meshullam, Berechiah’s son, worked in front of his own living area.

The next part was done by Malchijah, a goldsmith. He worked up to the building used by the temple servants and the traders. That was across from the Inspection Gate, and his work reached the upper room at the corner.{l}
The last stretch, between that corner room and the Sheep Gate, was fixed by the goldsmiths and the traders.

notes.text: The Hebrew calls it the Tower of Hammeah. The name may mean it was 100 cubits high, about 150 feet (45 meters), or that it had 100 steps. Hananel means “God is kind.”
Or “their Lord.”
Or “the Jeshanah Gate,” named for the town of Jeshanah.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew verb is uncertain. It may mean “left,” “paved,” or “restored.”
The Hebrew says “1,000 cubits,” about 450 meters. It calls the gate the “Dung Gate.”
Shelah means “channel.” It is the pool fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel, called Siloam in John 9:7.
Some Hebrew copies, the Septuagint, and the Syriac say “Binnui” (see verse 24).
Some Hebrew copies say Zaccai. The word for “worked hard” is uncertain.
The Hebrew word may mean the Jordan Valley or the land around Jerusalem.
Ophel means “hill.” It was the ridge between David’s City and the temple hill.
The Hebrew calls it the Miphkad Gate.

verses.text: Sanballat found out we were rebuilding the wall, and he flew into a rage. He was furious, and he poured scorn on the Jews.{a}

In front of his friends and Samaria’s army he said, “What do these feeble Jews think they are doing? Can they put the city back by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Do they think they will be done in one day? Those stones are burned and buried in rubble. Do they expect them to come alive again?”
Tobiah from Ammon stood by his side. “Go ahead and let them build!” he said. “That stone wall of theirs is so weak that a fox could knock it down just by climbing on it!”
Hear us, our God! They look down on us. Let the shame they heap on us fall on them instead. Let them be carried off like loot into a land where they are prisoners.
Do not hide their guilt. Do not wipe their sin out of your sight. They have insulted you right in front of the builders.{b}
So we kept building the wall. Soon it was joined all the way around, up to half its height. The people’s hearts were set on the work.

Sanballat and Tobiah got word that the repairs on Jerusalem’s walls were going forward and the broken places were being filled. So did the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the men of Ashdod. Their anger burned hot.
Together they plotted to march on Jerusalem, attack it, and stir up chaos there.
Our answer was prayer to our God. Day and night we also kept a guard posted against them.
Meanwhile, in Judah people were saying, “The men carrying loads have no strength left. The rubble is piled too high. We will never be able to finish this wall.”
Our enemies were saying, “They will not know or see a thing until we are right among them. Then we will kill them and put an end to the work.”
Jews who lived near the enemies came to us again and again, ten times over. “Wherever you turn,” they said, “they will come at us from every side.”{c}
So in the low places behind the wall, where it was open, I put people on guard by families. They held swords, spears, and bows.{d}

After I had looked things over, I stood up to speak. My words were for everyone, from the leading families and officials to all the ordinary people. “Don’t be scared of them!” I said. “Keep your minds on the Lord, who is great and fills us with awe. Fight for your relatives, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes!”{e}
Word came to our enemies that their plot was no secret to us. God had spoiled what they planned. Then every one of us went back to the wall, each person to his own task.{f}

After that, I split my men into two groups. One group did the building. The other group held spears, shields, bows, and armor, ready to fight. The commanders took their places behind all of Judah’s people
as they rebuilt the wall. Those who hauled loads kept one hand on their work and gripped a weapon with the other.
Every builder wore his sword at his belt while he built. Beside me stood the trumpeter.
Then I told the important families, the officials, and everyone else, “The work is huge and spread out. We are scattered along the wall, a long way from each other.
When you hear the trumpet, run to the place it is coming from and join us there. Our God will do our fighting!”
So the work went on, while half the men kept spears in hand. Morning light to starlight, we never stopped.
I also told the people then, “Each man and his helper must stay inside Jerusalem overnight. That way they can stand guard at night and work during the day.”
None of us ever changed clothes, not I, not my brothers, not my men, not the guards with me. Each of us kept his weapon in his hand.{g}

notes.text: In the Hebrew Bible, verses 1-6 are numbered 3:33-38, and verses 7-23 are numbered 4:1-17. The CTB uses the usual English numbers.
Or “they have thrown insults at the builders.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
Some Hebrew copies spell this word differently.
The Hebrew word is Adonai.
Some Hebrew copies say “and we will go back.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. It says “each his weapon, the water.”

verses.text: About that time, a loud outcry rose up. Men and their wives were complaining against their fellow Jews.
Some said, “Our families are large, with many sons and daughters. We need grain to eat, or we will not stay alive.”
Others said, “Food is scarce. To get grain, we have had to give our fields, vineyards, and homes as a promise that we will pay.”
Still others said, “To pay what the king demands on our fields and vineyards, we have had to borrow money.

We belong to the same people as everyone else here. Our children are as precious as theirs. Yet our own sons and daughters are being made slaves. Some of our girls already belong to masters. We can do nothing about it, because our fields and vineyards now belong to other men.”
When I heard their cries and what they said, I was furious.
I thought it through. Then I accused the important families and officials. “You are lending to your own people and taking interest from them!” I said. A large gathering was called to face them.{a}

I told them, “We have done all we could to buy back our fellow Jews who were sold to other nations. Now you are selling your own relatives! Will they have to be sold back to us?” They had nothing to say. They could not think of a single answer.
I went on, “What you are doing is wrong. You should live in fear of our God! Then our enemies, the other nations, would have no reason to mock us.{b}
My brothers, my men, and I have also been lending the people money and grain. Let us all stop charging interest!

Today, right now, give back their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses. Also return what you have been charging them, the interest on their loans of money and grain, of new wine and olive oil.”{c}

“Everything will be returned,” they said. “We will not ask them for anything more. Whatever you say, we will do.” So I sent for the priests. I had the leaders make an oath in front of them to keep this promise.

Then I took the folded part of my robe and shook it hard. “Any man who breaks this promise,” I said, “God will shake like this, right out of his home and away from all he has worked for. Let him be shaken out and left with nothing!” The whole group said, “Amen!” They praised Yahweh. And the people did what they had promised.

I was made governor in Judah in King Artaxerxes’s twentieth year. I served for twelve years, until his thirty-second year. In all that time, neither I nor my relatives ate the food the governor was allowed to receive.{d}

Earlier governors had made life hard for the people. They demanded bread and wine and about a pound of silver. Their helpers also bullied the people. I acted differently out of respect and fear for God.{e}
Instead, I put my effort into rebuilding the wall. We did not buy any land. All my men gathered there to work.
Every day 150 Jews and officials ate at my table. That did not count the visitors from the nations around us.

Each day I paid for an ox, six choice sheep, and poultry to be cooked. Every ten days I provided plenty of all kinds of wine. Yet I never asked for the governor’s food allowance, because the people already carried such a heavy load.
Remember me, my God, and be good to me because of all I have done for these people.

notes.text: The Hebrew may mean “taking a pledge” or “charging interest.”
Some Hebrew copies say “and he said.”
The Hebrew says “the hundredth,” probably one percent a month.
This was from 445 to 433 BC.
The Hebrew says “40 shekels of silver,” about 1 pound (460 grams). This was probably a daily charge.

verses.text: Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and our other enemies learned that I had finished rebuilding the wall. Not one gap was left, though the gates were still waiting for their doors.
Then a message came to me from Sanballat and Geshem. “Come and meet with us,” it said, “in one of the villages on the plain of Ono.” But their real plan was to hurt me.{a}
I sent messengers back with my answer. “I am busy with a great project,” I told them. “I cannot come down there. Why should the work stop just so I can leave it to visit you?”
Four times they sent me the same message. Each time, I gave them the same reply.
Sanballat tried a fifth time. He sent his servant with the same request, but this time he carried an open letter.

This is what it said: “People in the nations around here are saying, and Gashmu agrees, that you and the Jews plan to rebel. They say your wall is meant for that. These reports also say you plan to make yourself their king.{b}
They say you have even chosen prophets to announce in Jerusalem, ‘Judah has a king!’ The king will surely hear about this. So come, and let us talk it over together.”
I sent him this answer: “None of what you say is true. You are making it all up.”
They all hoped to make us afraid. “They will give up,” they thought. “The work will never get done.” But I prayed, “Now make my hands strong!”{c}

One day I went to see Shemaiah. He was the son of Delaiah and grandson of Mehetabel, and he had shut himself up at home. He said, “Let us meet at God’s house, inside the temple. Let us close the temple doors. Men are coming to kill you. They are coming tonight to kill you!”
But I answered, “Would a man in my position run and hide? Could a man like me enter the temple and live? No, I refuse to go in there!”{d}
Then it became clear to me. God had not sent this man. He had given this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
They had paid him to frighten me, so that I would sin by doing what he said. Then they could ruin my good name and shame me.
My God, do not forget the deeds of Tobiah and Sanballat. Do not forget Noadiah, the woman prophet, or the rest of the prophets who wanted me to be afraid.
The wall was completed in fifty-two days. It was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Elul (in August–September).{e}
Every enemy we had got the news. The nations living around us grew afraid and felt very small. They knew that our God had helped us do this work.
During those days, Judah’s important men sent many letters to Tobiah, and his letters kept coming back to them.

A lot of people in Judah had taken an oath to stand by him. Tobiah had married into the family of Shecaniah, Arah’s son. And Tobiah’s son Jehohanan had married a daughter of Meshullam, whose father was Berechiah.
They kept praising Tobiah’s good deeds to my face. Then they repeated to him everything I said. Meanwhile Tobiah wrote me letter after letter to make me afraid.

notes.text: The Hebrew may also mean “at Hakkephirim.”
Gashmu is another form of the name Geshem.
This is a short prayer. The Septuagint says “So now I made my hands strong.”
Nehemiah was not a priest. Only priests could enter the temple building (Numbers 18:7).
Elul was the sixth month. In 445 BC its twenty-fifth day was about the start of October. So the work began early in the fifth month, Av (in July–August).

verses.text: The wall was finished, and I had hung its doors. The gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were given their jobs.

Then I put two men in charge of Jerusalem. One was my brother Hanani. The other was Hananiah, commander of the fortress. Hananiah was a man of his word, and few people had as much reverence for God as he did.

I gave them orders. “Do not open Jerusalem’s gates until the sun is high and hot,” I said. “Even while the gatekeepers stand at their posts, the doors must be closed and locked tight. Choose guards from among the people who live in Jerusalem. Put some at guard posts, and have others watch near their own houses.”{a}
The city was wide and large, but only a few people lived there, and houses had not yet been rebuilt.

So my God gave me an idea. I would gather the important families, the officials, and the people, and have them listed by families. I came across the family record of those who had come back first. This is what it said:{b}
These people of the province came home from captivity. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried them away. Back they came to Jerusalem and Judah, every person going to the town that was his.
Their leaders were Zerubbabel and Jeshua, Nehemiah and Azariah, Raamiah and Nahamani, Mordecai and Bilshan, Mispereth and Bigvai, Nehum and Baanah. Here are the numbers of Israel’s men:{c}
From Parosh: 2,172.
From Shephatiah: 372.
From Arah: 652.
From Pahath-moab, through Jeshua and Joab: 2,818.
From Elam: 1,254.
Zattu’s descendants totaled 845.
Zaccai’s totaled 760.
Binnui’s totaled 648.
Bebai’s totaled 628.
Azgad’s totaled 2,322.
Adonikam’s line had 667.
Bigvai’s line had 2,067.
Adin’s line had 655.
Ater’s line, through Hezekiah, had 98.
Hashum’s people were 328.
Bezai’s people were 324.
Hariph’s people were 112.
Gibeon’s people were 95.
Now the towns. Bethlehem and Netophah together: 188 men.
Men of Anathoth numbered 128.
Beth-azmaveth had 42.
Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth had 743 together.
Ramah and Geba had 621.
There were 122 men of Michmas.
Bethel and Ai had 123.
The other Nebo had 52.
People of the other Elam numbered 1,254.
Harim had 320.
There were 345 men of Jericho.
Lod, Hadid, and Ono had 721.
Senaah had the most, 3,930.
These were the priests. Jedaiah’s descendants, from Jeshua’s family: 973.
Immer’s: 1,052.
Pashhur’s: 1,247.
Harim’s: 1,017.
There were 74 Levites. They came from Jeshua’s family, through Kadmiel and the line of Hodevah.
There were 148 singers, all from Asaph’s family.
There were 138 gatekeepers, from the families of Shallum and Ater, Talmon and Akkub, Hatita and Shobai.
The temple servants came from these families: Ziha, Hasupha, and Tabbaoth;
then Keros, Sia, and Padon;
then Lebana, Hagaba, and Shalmai;
then Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar;
then Reaiah, Rezin, and Nekoda;
then Gazzam, Uzza, and Paseah;
then Besai, Meunim, and Nephushesim;{d}
then Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harhur;
then Bazlith, Mehida, and Harsha;
then Barkos, Sisera, and Temah;
and last, Neziah and Hatipha.
Families descended from Solomon’s servants came as well: Sotai, Sophereth, and Perida;
then Jaala, Darkon, and Giddel;
then Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth-hazzebaim, and Amon.
Counting the temple servants with the families from Solomon’s servants, the total was 392.
Another group traveled from Tel-melah and Tel-harsha, from Cherub, Addon, and Immer. They had no way to prove that their families were part of Israel.
They were from the families of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, 642 in all.

Some priests could not prove their families either. They were from the families of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai. (That last man had married into the family of Barzillai from Gilead and was called by that family’s name.)
They hunted for their names in the family records, but no names turned up. So they were kept from serving as priests, because they were counted as unclean.
The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy food. They had to wait until a priest could ask God for an answer using the Urim and Thummim.{e}
Counting everyone together, the whole group came to 42,360.
On top of that, they had 7,337 male and female servants, and 245 men and women who sang.
They brought 736 horses and 245 mules,{f}
435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys.
Family leaders gave toward the work as well. The governor put into the treasury about 18 1/2 pounds of gold, 50 bowls, and 530 robes for priests.{g}
Some of the family leaders gave about 370 pounds of gold and about 1 1/3 tons of silver to the building fund.{h}
The rest of the people together gave about 370 pounds of gold, about 1 1/4 tons of silver, and 67 robes for priests.{i}

So the priests and Levites, the gatekeepers and singers, the temple servants, some of the people, and the rest of Israel made their homes in their own towns. When the seventh month (in September–October) came around, the Israelites were settled in their towns.{j}

notes.text: Some Hebrew copies say “and he said.”
Verses 6-73 repeat Ezra 2:1-70 with many small changes in names and numbers.
Ezra 2:2 has Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mispar, and Rehum for Azariah, Raamiah, Mispereth, and Nehum, and does not have Nahamani.
Some Hebrew copies say Nephushsim.
The Hebrew word for governor is Tirshatha, a Persian title (see Ezra 2:63).
Most Hebrew copies do not have this verse. It comes from some copies and from Ezra 2:66.
The Hebrew says “1,000 darics.” A daric was a Persian gold coin of about 0.3 ounce (8.4 grams).
The Hebrew says “20,000 darics” of gold and “2,200 minas” of silver. A mina was about 1 1/4 pounds (575 grams).
The Hebrew says “20,000 darics” of gold and “2,000 minas” of silver.
The seventh month was Tishri. This was the fall of 445 BC.

subheads.5: The Record of the First Returners

verses.text: Every one of the people came together as if they were one person. They met in the open square facing the Water Gate. They called on Ezra, the teacher of the Law, to bring the scroll with Moses’s Law in it, the Law Yahweh had given Israel.{a}
So Ezra the priest carried the Law out to the gathering. Men and women were there, and everyone old enough to understand. The date was the seventh month (in September–October), on its first day.{b}
Facing the square by the Water Gate, he read the scroll aloud from sunrise until noon. Men, women, and all who could understand heard it. Every ear was turned to the Book of the Law.

Ezra the teacher stood high on a wooden stand built for the purpose. Six men stood at his right hand: Mattithiah and Shema, Anaiah and Uriah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah. Seven stood at his left: Pedaiah and Mishael, Malchijah and Hashum, Hashbaddanah and Zechariah, and Meshullam.{c}
Since Ezra stood above the crowd, they could all watch him open the scroll. As soon as he opened it, the people rose to their feet.
Ezra praised Yahweh, the great God. Raising their hands, the people answered, “Amen! Amen!” Then they bent down low with their faces to the ground and worshiped Yahweh.

Some Levites helped the people understand the Law while everyone stayed standing in place. They were Jeshua, Bani, and Sherebiah; Jamin, Akkub, and Shabbethai; Hodiah, Maaseiah, and Kelita; Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah.
They read from God’s Law scroll and made it clear. They explained what it meant, so the people understood each part that was read.{d}

Tears had been running down people’s faces while the Law was read. So Nehemiah, who was governor, spoke up, together with Ezra, priest and teacher, and the Levites teaching the crowd. “Today is a holy day to Yahweh your God,” they said to all of them. “This is no time for grief or tears.”{e}
Nehemiah added, “Go home and eat a fine meal and drink something sweet. Share with those who have nothing prepared. Today is holy to our Lord. Do not be sad! Yahweh’s joy will make you strong.”{f}
The Levites moved through the crowd, quieting everyone. “Be still,” they said, “for this day is holy. Stop grieving.”
So all the people went off to eat and drink, to share food with others, and to celebrate with great joy. What had been read to them now made sense.
The next day the heads of all the families met with Ezra the teacher, along with the priests and the Levites. They wanted to learn more of what the Law said.
In the Law they found what Yahweh had commanded through Moses. During the festival in the seventh month, the Israelites were to live in shelters.{g}

They were also to spread this message through every town and through Jerusalem: “Head for the hills. Bring back branches from olive trees and wild olive trees, from myrtles, palms, and other trees thick with leaves. Make shelters with them, as the Law says.”

The people did it. They cut branches and carried them home. They built shelters on their flat roofs, in their courtyards, and in the courtyards of God’s house. Shelters went up in the open places near the Water Gate and near the Ephraim Gate as well.
Everyone back from captivity made a shelter and stayed in it. Not since Joshua son of Nun had Israel held such a festival. Their joy was enormous.{h}
Ezra read from the Book of God’s Law every day of the festival, start to finish. The celebration lasted seven days. Then came a special gathering on day eight, as the Law required.

notes.text: The Greek book 1 Esdras (9:37-55) tells this story too and ends with it.
This was the day of trumpet blasts (Leviticus 23:24). Later it became the Jewish New Year (Rosh Hashanah).
The Hebrew says “a tower of wood.”
Or “they translated it.” The Law may have been explained in Aramaic, the everyday language of the time.
The Hebrew word for governor is Tirshatha, a Persian title (see Ezra 2:63).
The Hebrew word is Adonai.
See Leviticus 23:33-43. The Festival of Shelters began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The Hebrew says “Jeshua,” a later form of the name Joshua.

subheads.9: A Day for Joy, Not Tears

verses.text: On the twenty-fourth day of that same month (in September–October), the Israelites met again. This time they went without food. They were dressed in sackcloth, with dirt sprinkled over them.{a}
Those of Israelite birth kept apart from all foreigners. Standing up, they admitted their own sins and the wrongs of their ancestors.
For about three hours they stood in place while the Book of the Law of Yahweh their God was read. Another three hours went to confessing sin and to bowing low in worship before Yahweh their God.{b}
Some Levites stood on the stairs: Jeshua, Bani, and Kadmiel; Shebaniah, Bunni, and Sherebiah; Bani and Chenani. With loud voices they cried out to Yahweh their God.

Then other Levites called out to the people. They were Jeshua and Kadmiel, Bani and Hashabneiah, Sherebiah and Hodiah, Shebaniah and Pethahiah. “Stand up!” they said. “Praise Yahweh your God, who lives forever and ever!” Then they prayed: “May your glorious name be praised! It is far greater than all the praise and blessing we can give.

“Yahweh, you are the only one. You made the skies and the highest heavens, with all their stars. The ground and all that covers it, the oceans and all that swims in them, are your work. All of them stay alive because of you. Heaven’s armies bow in worship to you.{c}
You are Yahweh, the God who picked out Abram. You led him out of Ur in Chaldea, and you gave him the name Abraham.{d}

You saw that his heart was faithful to you. So you made a solemn agreement with him. The land would go to his descendants, you said, the land where the Canaanites and Hittites lived, with the Amorites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites. You kept your word, for you are always in the right.
“In Egypt you saw how our ancestors were suffering. At the Red Sea you heard them cry out.{e}

You did miraculous signs and amazing things against Pharaoh, his officials, and everyone in his land. You knew how cruelly and proudly the Egyptians had treated our people. You made a name for yourself that people remember even now.
You opened a path through the sea for our ancestors. Down the middle they went, on dry ground. But those chasing them you hurled into the deep water. They sank like a stone in the raging waves.
In the daytime you led your people with a column of cloud. At night you used a column of fire to light up the path ahead of them.
You came down on Mount Sinai. From heaven your voice reached them. Your rulings were fair and your teaching true. Your laws and commands were good.
You taught them that the Sabbath was your holy day. Through Moses, who served you, you gave them commands, rules, and teachings.
Bread from heaven came from you when they were hungry. Water poured from a rock for them when they were thirsty. Then you sent them in to claim the land you had promised with an oath.
“But our ancestors became proud and stubborn. Your commands meant nothing to them.

They would not hear you. The miracles you had done for them slipped from their minds. They grew stubborn and turned against you. They even picked someone to lead them back to being slaves. But forgiving is your nature. You are kind and full of mercy. You are slow to get angry, and your faithful love is great. So you did not leave them.{f}
They even poured melted gold into the shape of a calf. ‘Here is your god,’ they said, ‘who led you up out of Egypt!’ What they said against you was shocking.
Yet because your mercy is so great, you did not leave them alone in the desert. The column of cloud kept guiding them by day along the way. The column of fire kept lighting their path by night.
Your good Spirit was your gift to them, to teach them. You kept feeding them manna. You gave them water to drink when they were thirsty.
Forty years you looked after them in the wilderness. They never lacked anything. Their clothes never wore out, and their feet never swelled up.
You handed kingdoms and nations over to them. You gave them each corner of the land. Sihon’s country, where the king of Heshbon ruled, became theirs, and so did the country of Og, Bashan’s king.{g}
Their children grew as countless as the stars overhead. You led them into the land that their fathers had been told they would enter and own.

So their children went in and took over the land. You crushed the Canaanites who lived there. You put them in your people’s power, along with their kings and the peoples of the land, to do with as they pleased.

Your people captured walled cities and rich farmland. They took over houses full of good things, wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and more fruit trees than they could count. They ate their fill and grew plump. They enjoyed all your great goodness.
“Even so, they disobeyed you and rebelled. They turned their backs on your Law. The prophets you sent pleaded with them to return to you, and they murdered them. They insulted you terribly.

So you let their enemies defeat them and make them suffer. But when they were in trouble, they cried out to you. From heaven you heard them. Because your mercy is so great, you sent them leaders who set them free from their enemies.

Yet once things were calm, they went right back to evil in front of you. Then you let their enemies take control of them. Again they called to you for help, and again heaven heard. Over and over, because of your mercy, you rescued them.

You kept urging them to come back to your Law. But they were proud and ignored your commands. They sinned against your rules, the rules that give life to anyone who obeys them. They turned away from you. They were stubborn and would not listen.{h}
Year after year you bore with them. Your Spirit spoke warnings to them by the mouths of your prophets. But they would not pay attention. So you let the nations around them take them over.
Even then, because your mercy is so great, you did not destroy them completely or leave them. Kindness and mercy are who you are, our God.

“So now, our God, you are great and mighty and awesome. You keep your promises and your faithful love. Do not treat our troubles as unimportant. Hardship has struck every one of us: kings, leaders, priests, prophets, our fathers, and the whole people. It has lasted from the days of the kings of Assyria until now.
In all that has come on us, you have been in the right. You kept faith with us; we were the ones who did evil.
Your Law was not kept by our kings or our leaders, by our priests or our ancestors. Your commands and your warnings meant nothing to them.
You gave them a kingdom of their own, many good things, and a wide, rich land. Even with all that, they did not serve you or turn from the evil they did.
So look at us now! Slaves is what we are today, right here in the land you handed to our ancestors to eat the fruit and good things that it grows.
The kings you set over us because of our sins now take its rich harvest. Whatever they please, they do with our bodies and our livestock. We are in deep trouble.
“So in light of all this, we are binding ourselves with a firm promise in writing. Our leaders, our Levites, and our priests are putting their seals on it.”{i}

notes.text: This was the seventh month, Tishri, two days after the Festival of Shelters ended.
The Hebrew says “a quarter of the day.”
The Septuagint begins this verse with “And Ezra said.”
Abram means “honored father.” Abraham means “father of many” (Genesis 17:5).
The Hebrew says Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Some Hebrew copies and the Septuagint say “to their slavery in Egypt” (see Numbers 14:4).
The Hebrew may also mean “the land of Sihon and the land of the king of Heshbon.”
See Leviticus 18:5.
In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 10:1.

subheads.9: Out of Egypt and Through the Desert

verses.text: The first name sealed on the document was Nehemiah the governor, Hacaliah’s son. Then came Zedekiah,{a}
and Seraiah with Azariah and Jeremiah,
and Pashhur with Amariah and Malchijah,
and Hattush with Shebaniah and Malluch,
and Harim with Meremoth and Obadiah,
and Daniel with Ginnethon and Baruch,
and Meshullam with Abijah and Mijamin,
and Maaziah with Bilgai and Shemaiah. All of these were priests.
Next came the Levites. Jeshua was Azaniah’s son. Binnui came from Henadad’s family. Kadmiel signed too.
Their fellow Levites were Shebaniah and Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, and Hanan;
then Mica and Rehob, and Hashabiah;
then Zaccur and Sherebiah, and Shebaniah;
then Hodiah and Bani, and Beninu.
Then came the leaders of the people. Parosh, Pahath-moab, and Elam were first, then Zattu and Bani;
after them Bunni and Azgad, and Bebai;
after them Adonijah and Bigvai, and Adin;
after them Ater and Hezekiah, and Azzur;
after them Hodiah and Hashum, and Bezai;
after them Hariph and Anathoth, and Nebai;{b}
after them Magpiash and Meshullam, and Hezir;
after them Meshezabel and Zadok, and Jaddua;
after them Pelatiah and Hanan, and Anaiah;
after them Hoshea and Hananiah, and Hasshub;
after them Hallohesh and Pilha, and Shobek;
after them Rehum and Hashabnah, and Maaseiah;
after them Ahiah and Hanan, and Anan;
and last, Malluch and Harim, and Baanah.

The rest of the people joined in too. That included the priests and Levites, the gatekeepers and singers, and the temple servants. It included everyone who had turned away from the nations around them to obey God’s Law. Their wives came too, with every son and daughter old enough to understand.

All of them stood with their relatives and their leaders. They swore an oath and called a curse on themselves if they failed. They promised to live by God’s Law, which he gave through Moses, his servant. They promised to keep every command of Yahweh our Lord, with all his rules and laws.{c}
“Our daughters will not marry men from the peoples around us,” they said. “Our sons will not marry their daughters.

On the Sabbath, the peoples around us may bring goods or grain to sell. On that day, and on every holy day, we will buy nothing from them. In the seventh year our land will lie unplowed, and all debts will be wiped away.{d}
“We also take on the duty of giving about 1/8 ounce of silver each year. It will pay for the work of our God’s house.{e}

It will pay for the holy bread that is set out. It will supply the grain and burnt offerings made every day, and those made on Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals. It will cover the holy gifts and the sin offerings that make peace with God for Israel. It will cover all the work at our God’s house.

“Lots have been drawn among priests, Levites, and people to set the times each family will deliver wood to our God’s house. The wood will be brought at set times every year to burn on the altar of Yahweh our God, as the Law says.
“Every year we will bring to Yahweh’s house the first part of what our land grows. We will bring the first fruit from every tree.

“As the Law says, we will bring our firstborn sons to our God’s house. We will bring the firstborn of our cattle, sheep, and goats there too. The priests on duty in the house of our God will receive them.

“We will bring the first of our ground meal and our other gifts to the priests, to the storerooms of our God’s house. Fruit from all our trees will come too, with new wine and olive oil. We will give a tenth of our crops to the Levites. In every farming town, they are the ones who gather that tenth.{f}
A priest from Aaron’s family will go with the Levites when they collect the tenth. The Levites must take a tenth of what they collect to our God’s house and put it in the storerooms.

The people of Israel and the Levites must carry their gifts of grain, new wine, and olive oil into those storage rooms. That is where the holy objects are kept and where the serving priests, the gatekeepers, and the singers stay. We will not neglect the house of our God.”

notes.text: The Hebrew says “On the sealed ones were.”
Some Hebrew copies say Nobai.
The Hebrew word is Adonai.
See Exodus 23:10-11 and Deuteronomy 15:1-2.
The Hebrew says “a third of a shekel,” about 4 grams. Exodus 30:13 had required half a shekel.
Or “dough.”

verses.text: Jerusalem became home to the people’s leaders. As for everyone else, lots were drawn. For every ten families, one would go and live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while nine stayed where they were.
The people thanked and blessed every man who offered on his own to live in Jerusalem.

Here are the province leaders who lived in Jerusalem. (In Judah’s towns, everyone lived on his own land in his own town. That included ordinary Israelites, priests, Levites, temple servants, and the families of Solomon’s servants.){a}
Some people from Judah and some from Benjamin settled in Jerusalem. From Judah there was Athaiah. His line went back through Uzziah, Zechariah, Amariah, Shephatiah, and Mahalalel to Perez.
There was also Maaseiah. His line went back through Baruch, Col-hozeh, Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib, and Zechariah to Shelah’s family.{b}
Perez’s descendants who lived in Jerusalem numbered 468 brave men.
From Benjamin there was Sallu. His line went back through Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah, and Ithiel to Jeshaiah.
His followers, Gabbai and Sallai, and others brought the number to 928.{c}
Joel, Zichri’s son, was the officer over them. Judah, Hassenuah’s son, ranked next over the city’s affairs.
From the priests there was Jedaiah, Joiarib’s son, and Jachin.
There was Seraiah, the chief officer of God’s house. His line went back through Hilkiah, Meshullam, Zadok, and Meraioth to Ahitub.
Their fellow priests who worked in the temple numbered 822. There was Adaiah. His line went back through Jeroham, Pelaliah, Amzi, Zechariah, and Pashhur to Malchijah.
His relatives, who were heads of families, numbered 242. There was Amashsai. His line went back through Azarel, Ahzai, and Meshillemoth to Immer.
With them were 128 of their brave fighting men. Their officer was Zabdiel, Haggedolim’s son.{d}
From the Levites there was Shemaiah. His line went back through Hasshub, Azrikam, and Hashabiah to Bunni.
Shabbethai and Jozabad, two Levite leaders, were in charge of the outside work of God’s house.

Mattaniah led the prayers of thanks. His father was Mica, his grandfather Zabdi, and his ancestor Asaph. Bakbukiah came second among his relatives. There was also Abda, whose line went back through Shammua and Galal to Jeduthun.{e}
The holy city had 284 Levites living in it altogether.
Akkub and Talmon led the gatekeepers, along with their relatives. They stood guard at the gates, 172 of them.
Everyone else from Israel, priests and Levites included, made homes in Judah’s many towns. Each lived on the land his family owned.
Ophel hill was where the temple servants lived. Their supervisors were Ziha and Gishpa.

Uzzi was the officer over the Levites in Jerusalem. He was Bani’s son. His line went back through Hashabiah, Mattaniah, and Mica. He was from Asaph’s family, the singers who led the music in God’s house.
The king had given orders about the singers. Rules set out what they were to receive each day.
Pethahiah was Meshezabel’s son. He came from the clan of Zerah, one of Judah’s sons. He was the king’s helper in everything that had to do with the people.{f}
Some of Judah’s people lived in villages with farmland around them. Some lived in Kiriath-arba and nearby villages. Others lived at Dibon or at Jekabzeel, with the villages around each.{g}
Some lived in Jeshua, in Moladah, and in Beth-pelet.
Hazar-shual had some of them, and so did Beersheba with the villages around it.
Still others lived in Ziklag, and in Meconah and its villages.
Some were in En-rimmon, some in Zorah, some in Jarmuth.
There were others in Zanoah and Adullam and the villages near them, in Lachish and its fields, and in Azekah and its villages. So they lived all the way from Beersheba to Hinnom Valley.
The people of Benjamin lived starting from Geba. They were in Michmash, Aija, and Bethel with its villages.{h}
They lived in Anathoth and Nob, and in Ananiah,
in Hazor and Ramah, and in Gittaim,
in Hadid and Zeboim, and in Neballat,
in Lod, and in Ono, the Valley of Craftsmen.{i}
Some groups of Levites who had lived in Judah moved to Benjamin.

notes.text: Verses 3-19 are much like 1 Chronicles 9:2-17, with many differences.
The Hebrew says “the Shilonite.” It probably means a descendant of Shelah, Judah’s son (Numbers 26:20).
The Hebrew is uncertain. Some read “and his brothers, brave men.”
Or “son of the great ones,” meaning from a leading family.
Some Hebrew copies say Jedithun.
The Hebrew says “at the king’s hand.”
Kiriath-arba was the older name of Hebron (Genesis 23:2). It means “town of four” or “town of Arba.”
Or “The people of Benjamin from Geba lived at Michmash.”
The Hebrew calls it Ge-harashim.

verses.text: These priests and Levites made the journey back with Zerubbabel, whose father was Shealtiel, and with Jeshua. There were Seraiah and Jeremiah, and Ezra;
then Amariah and Malluch, and Hattush;
then Shecaniah and Rehum, and Meremoth;
then Iddo and Ginnethoi, and Abijah;
then Mijamin and Maadiah, and Bilgah;
then Shemaiah and Joiarib, and Jedaiah;
and last, Sallu and Amok, Hilkiah and Jedaiah. In Jeshua’s time as high priest, these men led the priests and their relatives.
The Levites were Jeshua and Binnui, Kadmiel and Sherebiah, Judah and Mattaniah. Mattaniah and his relatives led the songs of thanks.
Their relatives Bakbukiah and Unni stood facing them in groups during the services.{a}
Jeshua was the father of Joiakim. Joiakim was the father of Eliashib. Eliashib was the father of Joiada.
Joiada had a son named Jonathan, and Jonathan had a son named Jaddua.{b}
While Joiakim was high priest, these priests led the priestly families. Seraiah’s family was led by Meraiah. Jeremiah’s was led by Hananiah.
Ezra’s had Meshullam. Amariah’s had Jehohanan.
For Melicu’s there was Jonathan. For Shebaniah’s there was Joseph.{c}
Harim’s had Adna at its head. Meraioth’s had Helkai.
Iddo’s had Zechariah. Ginnethon’s had Meshullam.{d}
Abijah’s had Zichri. Miniamin’s and Moadiah’s had Piltai.{e}
Bilgah’s leader was Shammua. Shemaiah’s leader was Jehonathan.
Joiarib’s leader was Mattenai. Jedaiah’s leader was Uzzi.
Sallai’s was Kallai. Amok’s was Eber.
Hilkiah’s was Hashabiah. Jedaiah’s was Nethanel.
Records were kept of the heads of the Levite families while Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and then Jaddua served. The priests were recorded as well, up to the time when Darius the Persian ruled.{f}
The heads of the Levite families were written in the official record book, up to the days of Johanan, Eliashib’s son.

The Levite leaders were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua, Kadmiel’s son. Their relatives stood across from them. One group answered the other as they praised God and thanked him, just as David, the man of God, had ordered.
Six gatekeepers watched over the storerooms by the gates: Mattaniah and Bakbukiah, Obadiah and Meshullam, Talmon and Akkub.
Their service took place when Joiakim was high priest. He was Jeshua’s son and Jozadak’s grandson. They also served while Nehemiah was governor and while Ezra was priest and teacher of the Law.

Then the time came to dedicate Jerusalem’s wall. From every place they lived, the Levites were found and brought into the city. They came to celebrate the dedication with joy, singing songs of thanks and playing cymbals, harps, and lyres.
The singers came together too. They came from the area around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites.
Others came from Beth-gilgal and from the farmland near Geba and Azmaveth. Over time, the singers had settled in villages that ringed Jerusalem.
Priests and Levites first went through the ceremony to make themselves clean before God. Then they made the people, the gates, and the wall clean too.
I had Judah’s leaders climb up on top of the wall. I also put together two large choirs to march and give thanks. One choir went to the right along the top of the wall, toward the Garbage Gate.{g}
Hoshaiah followed them, along with half of Judah’s leaders.
Behind them came Azariah and Ezra, and Meshullam,
then Judah and Benjamin, and Shemaiah and Jeremiah.
Some young priests came next, blowing trumpets. One was Zechariah. His line went back through Jonathan, Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Micaiah, and Zaccur to Asaph.

Zechariah’s relatives played the instruments David, the man of God, had made. They were Shemaiah and Azarel, Milalai and Gilalai, Maai and Nethanel, Judah and Hanani. At the head of this group walked Ezra, the Law teacher.

When they reached the Fountain Gate, they climbed the steps of David’s City straight ahead. They climbed where the wall rises above David’s palace. Then they went on to the Water Gate on the east side.
The second choir went the other way, to the left. I walked behind it along the top of the wall, and half the people came too. We passed the Tower of the Ovens and went to the Wide Wall.{h}
We went over the Ephraim Gate, past the Old Gate, and by the Fish Gate. We passed Hananel’s Tower and the Hundred Tower and went on to the Sheep Gate. We stopped at the Guard Gate.{i}
Then both choirs that gave thanks took their places in God’s house. I stood there as well, along with half of the officials who were with me.
With us were these priests holding trumpets: Eliakim and Maaseiah, Miniamin and Micaiah, Elioenai and Zechariah, and Hananiah.
There were also Maaseiah and Shemaiah, Eleazar and Uzzi, Jehohanan and Malchijah, Elam and Ezer. The singers sang out loudly, led by Jezrahiah.

Many sacrifices were offered that day, and there was great celebration, for God had filled them with joy. The women and children joined in too. People far away could hear the joyful noise coming from Jerusalem.

On that same day, men were put in charge of the storerooms. These rooms held the gifts, the first part of the harvest, and the tenth of crops. Out of the farmland around each town, the men were to collect the shares the Law set aside for the priests and Levites. Judah was delighted with the priests and Levites who served.
These men did the work God gave them and kept things clean and holy. The singers and gatekeepers did their work too, as David and his son Solomon had ordered.
Long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, the singers had leaders. Even then, songs were sung to praise God and thank him.{j}

So all through the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, Israel supplied what the singers and gatekeepers needed each day. They also set aside a share for the Levites, and the Levites set aside a share for Aaron’s descendants.

notes.text: Some Hebrew copies say Unno. The Hebrew may mean “for watches.”
Jaddua was high priest about 330 BC. Jonathan here is probably the Johanan of verses 22-23.
Some Hebrew copies say Malluchi (see Malluch in verse 2).
Some Hebrew copies say Iddi.
A name seems to be missing from the Hebrew here.
This was probably Darius II, king of Persia 423-404 BC.
Facing east, “to the right” means to the south. The Hebrew calls the gate the “Dung Gate.”
The Hebrew says “to the front.” The Septuagint and other old versions say “to the left,” meaning to the north.
Or “the Jeshanah Gate” (see 3:6).
Some Hebrew copies say “a leader.”

subheads.1: Priests and Levites Who First Returned

verses.text: That same day, someone read from Moses’s book while the people listened. They came to a part that said no Ammonite or Moabite was ever to join God’s people when they gathered for worship.
The reason was that those nations had refused to meet Israel with bread and water. Instead they hired Balaam to speak a curse against Israel. Our God, though, turned that curse into a blessing.{a}
After hearing this part of the Law, the people sent away from Israel all who had foreign ancestors.
Some time before that, Eliashib the priest had been put in charge of the storerooms in our God’s house. He was a relative of Tobiah.

He had cleared out a large room for Tobiah to use. Before that, the room had held the grain offerings and incense, along with the temple objects. It also held the tenth of grain, new wine, and olive oil that God commanded for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the gifts for the priests.

All this went on while I was away from Jerusalem. In the thirty-second year that Artaxerxes ruled as king of Babylon, I had gone back to him. After a while I asked the king for permission to leave.{b}
When I returned to Jerusalem, I found out about the evil thing Eliashib had done. He had given Tobiah a room inside the courtyards of God’s house!
I was furious. I threw every bit of Tobiah’s furniture and belongings out of that room.
Then I gave orders, and the rooms were made clean again. I had the objects from God’s house put back in, along with the grain offerings and incense.

Something else came to my attention. The shares owed to the Levites had never been handed over. Because of that, the Levites and singers who led the worship had all left. Each had gone back to work his own fields.
So I scolded the officials. “Why is God’s house being neglected?” I asked them. Then I brought the Levites and singers back together and put them back at their jobs.
After that, all Judah brought a tenth of their grain, new wine, and olive oil to the storerooms again.

Over the storerooms I placed three men I could trust: Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the record keeper, and Pedaiah, a Levite. Hanan, son of Zaccur and grandson of Mattaniah, was their helper. These men were known to be honest. It was their job to hand out the supplies to their fellow workers.
My God, remember me for this! Keep in mind the loyal things I did for your house and for the worship held there.

Around that time I noticed people in Judah working on the Sabbath. Some were stomping grapes in winepresses. Others were bringing in grain and loading it on donkeys. They brought wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of other loads into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. I spoke out against their selling food on the day of rest.
Some men from Tyre had settled in Jerusalem. They carried in fish and every sort of goods for sale, and on the Sabbath they sold them to Judah’s people, right in Jerusalem.
So I faced Judah’s leading men and scolded them. “What is this evil you are doing?” I said. “You are treating the Sabbath day as if it were not holy!

Isn’t this just what your ancestors did? That is why our God brought all this trouble on us and on this city. And now, by treating the Sabbath as ordinary, you are stirring up even more of God’s anger against Israel!”

So I gave an order. Each Friday evening, as the shadows fell over Jerusalem’s gates before the Sabbath began, the doors were to be shut. They had to stay shut until the Sabbath was over. My own servants stood guard at the gates, so that nothing could be carried in on the Sabbath.
Once or twice the traders and people selling all kinds of goods spent the night camped outside Jerusalem.
But I warned them. “Why are you camping by the wall?” I said. “Do it again, and I will use force against you!” From then on, the Sabbath saw no more of them.

Then I ordered the Levites to make themselves clean and to come guard the gates. That way the Sabbath day would be kept holy. My God, remember me for this too. Show me mercy, because your faithful love is so great.
I also found Jewish men in those days who had taken wives from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.
Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of some other people. Not one of them knew how to talk in Judah’s own language.{c}

I argued with those men and called down curses on them. Some of them I struck, and I yanked hair from their heads. I had them take an oath in God’s name. “Your daughters must not become wives for their sons,” I said. “Do not take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves.

Wasn’t this how Solomon, king of Israel, fell into sin? Of all the nations, not one had a king like him. God loved him and gave him the throne of all Israel. Yet even Solomon was led into sin by women from foreign lands!{d}
Now must we hear that you are doing this same terrible evil? Will you break faith with our God by taking foreign wives?”
Eliashib the high priest had a grandson through his son Joiada. This grandson had become Sanballat the Horonite’s son-in-law. So I chased him away from me.
My God, remember them! They have made the priesthood unclean. They have broken the promise made with the priests and the Levites.
So I made the priests and Levites clean, removing everything foreign. I gave them their duties, each man with his own job.
I also arranged for wood to be brought at set times and for the first part of the harvest. My God, remember me and be good to me.

This was 433-432 BC. The Persian king was also called the king of Babylon.
The Hebrew says “Jewish,” meaning the language of Judah, which was Hebrew (see 2 Kings 18:26).
